paragraphs: A) Rabbi Zeira calls him “the Rav from Babylonia.” Rashi, Berakhot 46a, explains: this is the ordinarily mentioned Rav Huna. Because Rabbi Zeira had gone up from Babylonia and was now in the Land of Israel, he called him this. He lived in Derokart: Taanit 21b.

B) Yuchasin writes in his objections to the author of Dorot Olam, as follows: the author of Dorot Olam wrote that Rabbi Yehudah was greater than Rav Huna in wisdom. But I say [וא״א] that Rav Huna was wiser. The proof is Moed Katan 28a: Rava said, “I requested three things: Rav Huna’s wisdom, and it was granted me; Rav Chisda’s wealth, and it was granted me; Rabbah bar Rav Huna’s humility, and it was not granted me.” Since he requested Rav Huna’s wisdom rather than Rav Yehudah’s, it follows that Rav Huna was wiser than he. Perhaps he did not request Rav Yehudah’s wisdom because Rava was born on the day Rav Yehudah died. However, below I have written in Tosafot’s name that Rav Huna died before Rav Yehudah; thus Rava did not see Rav Huna, yet still requested his wisdom. But there is no need for proof from Moed Katan’s “I requested three things,” for below I have written in Tosafot’s name that Rav Huna was greater even than Shmuel, Rav Yehudah’s teacher. Moreover, we say in Berakhot that when Rav Yehudah reached Uktzin he said, “I see here the discussions of Rav and Shmuel.” Presumably he was not so wise; although Shmuel called him shinnana, “sharp one” (see his entry), perhaps he was sharp in comparison with the other students. Therefore the academy of Surya, where Rav Huna was, gained ascendancy. Rav Huna was wise, wealthy, and close to the patriarch. In Rav Sherira Gaon’s name: he was among the patriarchal descendants (see above). In his own entry, citing Dorot Olam, he wrote that he was close to the exilarch. See Gittin 11b: Rav Huna and Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef sat before Rabbi Yirmeyah. (Likewise in Shabbat 63b, Ravin and Rav Huna sat before Rabbi Yirmeyah; more explicitly in Zevachim 75b, Rav Huna and Rabbi Chizkiyah are Rabbi Yirmeyah’s students.) Tosafot writes there that this is not the Rav Huna mentioned without qualification throughout the Talmud, because Rabbi Zeira, Rav Yehudah’s student, was greater than Rabbi Yirmeyah, while Shmuel, Rav Yehudah’s teacher, needed Rav Huna, as we say at the beginning of our chapter, 5, and in Chullin 13 Shmuel asks Rav Huna; likewise Zevachim 46b. This implies that Shmuel was lesser than Rav Huna. How, then, did Rav Huna sit before Rabbi Yirmeyah, who called him “youngsters”? Tosafot likewise writes in Chullin 13: “It implies that Shmuel was lesser than Rav Huna. In Arakhin 16, Rav Huna and Chiyya bar Rav sat before Shmuel, implying a student before his teacher. In Gittin chapter 1, 11, Rav Huna sat before Rabbi Yirmeyah. Rabbi Yirmeyah was Rabbi Zeira’s colleague (see his entry); Rabbi Zeira was Rav Yehudah’s student, and Rav Yehudah was a student of Rav and Shmuel. Rabbi Yirmeyah called Rav Huna ‘youngsters.’ One may say there were two Rav Hunas. Nevertheless, the aforementioned one in Arakhin must have been Rav’s student.” End of quotation. See Berakhot 49a: Rabbi Zeira sat behind Rabbi Giddel before Rav Huna; there, 39a, Rabbi Zeira said, “When I was in Rav Huna’s house ….” Yuchasin writes: “Sefer Halikhot Olam writes that there were two Rav Hunas because we find Shmuel asking Rav Huna, as above. This is not convincing: since they deferred to him, although he was his student, he asked him; we find many instances in the Talmud of a teacher asking his student (see the introduction, among the rules). It is thus possible that he is one, without a second. This requires examination in light of Tosafot’s statement that Rav Huna, Rav’s student, sat before Shmuel in Arakhin. Thus Shmuel was his teacher; and this Rav Huna, Rav’s student, sat before Rabbi Yirmeyah and was Rabbi Yirmeyah’s student, while Rabbi Zeira sat before Rav Huna. How can these matters fit together? Perhaps the Rav Huna whom Shmuel asked was Rav Huna the exilarch in Babylonia, who died during Rabbi’s lifetime. Shmuel was alive then, for he was Rabbi’s physician. In Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam, gate 3, section 20: Rav Huna was Shmuel’s peer. If there are two, there must necessarily be three: one greater than Shmuel, one lesser, and the third lesser than Rabbi Yirmeyah, since Gittin chapter 1 says Rav Huna sat before Rabbi Yirmeyah.” End of quotation. Yuchasin writes that unqualified Rav Yirmeyah is Rav Huna’s student, in Kiddushin chapter 2. But I saw there, 45b, Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba. In Chullin 14a, Rav Huna said: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav expounded in Rav’s name. Tosafot writes: “This is puzzling, for in several places it implies that Rav Huna was greater than he: Arakhin 16b, where Rav Huna would trouble Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav by striking him; and Bekhorot 22a, Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav said to Rav Huna, ‘My teacher, explain your words.’” End of quotation. It is puzzling why they did not raise this difficulty concerning Ketubbot 22b, where Rav Huna asked Chiyya of Rav’s house. Moreover, the aforementioned Tosafot writes that there were two Rav Hunas. In Asheri, chapter Keitzad Meabberin, we rule like Rav Huna, because he was greater than Chiyya bar Rav. Rav Huna read in the priest’s place although he was not a priest, for even Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi, distinguished priests of the Land of Israel, deferred to him: Megillah 22a; Gittin 59b. But Jerusalem Talmud, Maaser Sheni chapter 5, halakhah 5, requires examination: Rav Huna did not take the tithe, suggesting that he was a priest, as it brings several there who were priests and did not take the tithe (see above, Rav Huna, Zeira’s father). But Rav Assi was greater than Rav Huna (see his entry).

C) Dorot Olam writes: Rav Yehudah became head in Nehardea after Shmuel—see his entry, that he was in Pumbedita—and Rav Huna in Sura. (In Rav Huna’s own entry, Yuchasin expresses surprise at Rashi and Tosafot’s explanation in Eruvin, “62, ס, side b” [locator as printed], that Rav Huna was in Pumbedita. The truth is as Dorot Olam says, that he was in Sura. So too at the end of Sanhedrin chapter 1: the elder of Sura is Rav Huna; the elder of Pumbedita, Rav Yehudah; there, the Judges of Sura are Rav Huna and Rav Chisda. In Rav Sherira Gaon: Sura is Mata Mechasya. Sefer Keritot writes: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda exercised authority in Babylonia; Rav Chisda went to Mata Mechasya, where they made him academy head, and Rav Huna’s academy was in Nehardea. End of quotation. This is not so, as stated above.) Rav Yehudah died, and both academies reverted to Rav Huna; he was academy head for forty years and died in 4050 (see above, Rav Huna the exilarch). This is not so, for Rav Huna died in the year sixty [ס׳], and Rav Chisda succeeded him in Sura (see his entry). In their days Rabbi Ammi was academy head in the Land of Israel (see his entry). See part 1, after year 4234. Rabbi Huna was the first academy head in Babylonia, for forty years, and after him Rav Chisda for ten years. Further in Yuchasin: these are the distinctions by which Sura’s academy rose above Pumbedita’s. Initially, in Rav’s days, which were the end of the Tannaim and beginning of the Amoraim, there was not yet an academy in Babylonia. Its patriarchs were called only resh sidra, as we say: “Who is the head of the order in Babylonia?” He answered, “Abba Arikha,” who is Rav (see his entry). After Rav died they made an academy in Babylonia on the model of the Land of Israel: the academy of Sura. Rav Huna ruled there forty years and was the first of all the academy heads in Babylonia. After him was Rav Chisda for ten years. At the end of Rav Chisda’s days, Rabbah bar Nachmani went and made an academy in Pumbedita. From that day onward there was an academy in Pumbedita, the academy of the Exile (see his entry). In Yuchasin, in Rav Sherira Gaon’s name: Shmuel died in year 564—it should read 562—which is year 4010 from creation. His students were Rav Nachman in Nehardea (see Arukh, entry nehar) and Rav Yehudah in Pumbedita. After Shmuel, Rav Huna ruled; he was among the patriarchal descendants. He ruled forty years and spread much Torah, as we say in Ketubbot 106a: he expounded through thirteen amoraim, meaning interpreters. When the rabbis left Rav Huna’s house and shook out their garments, dust would rise and cover the day; in the West they would say, “They have now risen from Rav Huna the Babylonian’s academy.” See Maharit’s responsum: this appears an exaggeration. Moreover, Babylonia is north of the Land of Israel, as stated at the beginning of Gittin; thus even if the dust rose to heaven it would not cover the daylight, since the sun goes on the southern side during the day. It appears to mean that when daylight in the West was obscured by clouds or dust, they would say, “They have risen from Rav Huna’s academy”—that is, it resembles their having risen—and mention him in praise, saying that he had many students. End of quotation. Eight hundred rabbis remained of Rav Huna’s house—those who ate at his table, Rashi. In chapter Haba al Yevimto, 64b, Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, Rav Sheshet, Rav Chelbo, Rav Giddel, Rav Acha bar Chanina, and sixty elders became sterile from Rav Huna’s lectures, except Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov (see his entry). In Rav Huna’s days Rabbi Yochanan died in the Land of Israel, and Huna’s position grew very strong [the witness has ד״ה], since he was among the patriarchal descendants. Rav Yehudah was in Pumbedita with his students before him and would appear before Rav Huna from time to time; Rabbi Nachman was in Shilchi and Mechoza with the rabbis of Nehardea. We do not find Rav Nachman entering before Rav Huna, for in several places Rav Nachman says, “Huna our colleague”: Gittin 52b; Arakhin 22a; Bava Kamma 96b; Bava Metzia 15a; chapter Ellu Terefot 56a; Niddah 16a. Rav Nachman said, “Huna told me”: Bava Metzia 71a; Bava Batra 138b. Rav Nachman said, “Huna agrees with me”: Eruvin 42b. Rav Nachman said to Rav Huna, “Let the master say”: Beitzah 22b. Rav Huna’s study house was near Mata Mechasya, which is Sura; Rav Chisda was Rav Huna’s colleague—see his entry, whether he was his student or a student-colleague—and was in Sura. During Rav Huna’s years, Rav Chisda built the academy in year 640; Rav Huna died in year 608. There is a scribal error here: it writes that Rav Chisda built the academy in year 640 of the era of contracts, which is 4088 from creation, during Rav Huna’s years; yet it writes that Rav Huna died in year 608 of contracts, which is 4056 from creation. Perhaps it should read that Rav Chisda built the academy in year 600 of contracts, which is 4048 from creation, and Rav Huna died in 4056. (Shalshelet HaKabbalah, folio 34, writes that four years before Rav Huna’s death Rav Chisda built a study house for himself.) They brought his coffin up to the Land of Israel, as stated in chapter Ellu Megallechin …. Rav Yehudah lived two years after him; all the rabbis came before him in Pumbedita. Rav Yehudah died in year 610. Rav Chisda ruled after him in Sura ten years and died in year 420—it should read 620, which is 4068. Go and see: according to the aforementioned Dorot Olam, Rabbi Yehudah died first and Rav Huna ruled afterwards; according to the aforementioned Rav Sherira Gaon, Rav Huna died first and Rav Yehudah lived two years after him. I saw in Tosafot, Menachot 36a: “This is how we read: Rabbah said, ‘Rav Huna explained it to me,’ rather than Rava. Rava never saw Rav Huna, for Kiddushin 72 says that Rava was born on the day Rav Yehudah died, and Rav Huna died before Rav Yehudah, as is proved in Moed Katan 17a: when Rav Yehudah died, she said, ‘There is no great man like Rav Yehudah here.’ Rav Huna was greater in wisdom and number than all Rav’s students, as appears in the last chapter of Ketubbot.” End of quotation. (Beside it was written folio 111; nothing was found there. It appears that they intended what is stated in the last chapter of Ketubbot, 106a, that he expounded through the aforementioned thirteen interpreters.) Tosafot likewise writes at the beginning of Bekhorot chapter 2, 14a: “We read, ‘Rabbah said in Rav Huna’s name,’ for Rava did not see Rav Huna …. When Rav Yehudah died, Rav Huna had already died, since it says, ‘There is no great man like Rav Yehudah’; Rav Huna was greater even than Shmuel, Rav Yehudah’s teacher, since Shmuel asked him at the beginning of Gittin.” End of quotation. (See above what I wrote.) Thus it is explicit that Rav Sherira’s words stand firm and secure. It appears that Dorot Olam follows his view that Rav Yehudah was greater than Rav Huna. He therefore holds that Rav Yehudah died first and Rav Huna was alive; they could thus say, “There is no great man like Rav Yehudah,” since Rav Yehudah was greater than Rav Huna. Understand this.

D) In Bava Kamma, chapter Merubbeh, 80, side a, Rav Huna said in Rav’s name: “We have made ourselves in Babylonia like the Land of Israel concerning small livestock”—that it is forbidden to raise them. Rav Adda bar Ahavah said to Rav Huna, “What about yours?”—you have small livestock. He answered, “Chovah guards ours”—his wife’s name. (In the Arukh, Rav Tzemach reads Chovah with a kaf.) He said, “May she bury her children”—you rely on her, and she cannot guard them. Throughout Rav Adda bar Ahavah’s years, Rav Huna’s offspring from Chovah did not survive. Chiddushei Aggadot objects: in chapter Shenei Nezirim, 57b, Rav Adda bar Ahavah said to Rav Huna, “Who rounds the minor’s head?” Rav Huna answered, “Chovah.” Rav Adda bar Ahavah said, “May Chovah bury her children.” It says there that throughout Rav Adda bar Ahavah’s years Rav Huna’s offspring did not survive. He answers that both caused it; see what he wrote. Yuchasin writes: “Heaven forbid that he cursed; rather, he spoke gently or in astonishment: ‘Has she buried her children, that she has no one to round her young son’s head?’ It was inadvertent …, and they did not survive. It appears that Rav Huna already had his humble son Rabbah before this incident, because Rav Huna died before Rav Adda bar Ahavah, as Rashi explains”—I do not know where Rashi wrote this—“but in my opinion Rav Adda bar Ahavah died before Rav Huna.” This is not so: Rav Huna died before Rav Adda bar Ahavah, for I wrote above in Rav Sherira Gaon’s and Tosafot’s names that Rav Huna died before Rav Yehudah; Rava was born on the day Rav Yehudah died, and Rav Adda bar Ahavah died in Rava’s days; see his entry. Or his son Rabbah was from another wife. It seems to me that this is exact in “offspring from Chovah did not survive,” implying that Rav Huna’s offspring from another wife did survive (see what I wrote under Rav Adda bar Ahavah). At the end of Moed Katan, 25b, when they eulogized Rabbah bar Rav Huna: “A stock of the aged ascended from Babylonia, with a Torah scroll.” Rashi explains that Rav Huna was exilarch, superior to the patriarch in the Land of Israel (see there). This does not appear in the Talmud, Kiddushin 70, side a: Rav Yehudah went and asked Rav Huna whether he should go to Rav Nachman, who had summoned him. Rav Huna answered, “You need not go, for you are a great man.” Rashi explains: you are greater than he, because you are head in Pumbedita and Rav Nachman in Nehardea. He told him to go to Rav Nachman, the exilarch’s son-in-law, for his honor. Dorot Olam likewise writes that he was close to the exilarch. But the Gemara’s wording is, “Rather, because of the honor of the patriarchal house”—he is the exilarch’s judge and the patriarch’s son-in-law—“arise and go.” In Bava Batra 65a, Rav Nachman said to Rav Huna, “Is the law like us or like you?” He answered, “The law is like you, for judges are frequent, because of proximity to the exilarch.” The Gemara’s wording is: “The law is like you, for you are close to the exilarch’s gate, where judges are frequent.” Rashbam explains: you are close to the exilarch’s house; Rav Nachman was the patriarchal house’s son-in-law and frequented the judges’ place, where judges were common, and saw cases daily and how they ruled. In Sanhedrin chapter 1, 5a, when Rabbah bar Rav Huna disputed with the exilarch, he said, “I have not taken authorization from you, for I have taken it from my father and master Rav Huna; my father from Rav; Rav from Rabbi Chiyya; Rabbi Chiyya from Rabbi.” Rashi explains: “I am not subordinate to the exilarch.” His intention is to refute Rashi’s interpretation: Rav Huna was not exilarch. It cannot be thought that Rashi intended this Rabbah to be the son of Rav Huna the exilarch of Rabbi’s days, for he said, “I took authorization from my father, and my father from Rav.” It is known that Rav Huna the Babylonian was Rav’s student, whereas the earlier Rav Huna the exilarch, of Rabbi’s days, was not Rav’s student. Dorot Olam too writes that Rav Huna the Babylonian was close to the exilarch; Yuchasin, in his objections to Dorot Olam, writes that he was close to the patriarch, and in Rav Sherira Gaon’s name that he was among the patriarchal descendants, as above. It appears that Rashi follows his view that Rav Huna was in Pumbedita. Yuchasin writes in Rav Sherira Gaon’s name that from Second Temple times Pumbedita was the principal place of the Exile, as we learned in Rosh Hashanah, “Until he saw the Exile like a bonfire”; Abaye said, “The Exile is Pumbedita.” End of quotation. Therefore Rashi wrote that Rav Huna was exilarch. But I have already brought many places showing that Rav Huna was in Sura and was not exilarch. Understand this.

E) Rav Huna died suddenly, and they were troubled because it was a snatched-away death, until they said in Rav Huna’s own name that this applies to one who dies before reaching the age of strength. He testified falsely in writing, “Until they said in Rav Huna’s own name that this ….” This is the wording of the Gemara, Moed Katan 28a: “Rav Huna died suddenly. The rabbis were examining the matter. A pair”—two Torah scholars who had come—“from Adiabene taught them: they taught this only of one who has not reached the age of strength”—meaning eighty years—“but if he has reached the age of strength, this is death by a kiss; Rav Huna had reached that age.” Thus Rav Huna did not say it. There in Moed Katan 25a, when Rav Huna died, they thought to place a Torah scroll on his bier, in his honor, to say, “This man fulfilled what is written in this”; Rashi. Rav Chisda said to them: “A thing he did not accept during his lifetime …! For Rabbi Chelbo said”—this is Ein Yaakov’s reading, but the Gemara’s reading is Rabbi Tachlifa—“I saw Rav Huna wishing to sit on his bed while a Torah scroll lay on it; he inverted a jar, placed the Torah scroll on it, and then sat.” His bier would not go out through the doorway; they thought to lower it through the roofs. Rav Chisda said, “This is what I learned from him: a deceased sage’s honor is through the doorways.” They thought to transfer him from one bed to another; “This is how ….” Rabbi Abba opened his eulogy: “Our master was worthy that the Divine Presence should rest upon him, but Babylonia caused otherwise.” When they brought him up there, they told Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi, “Rav Huna has come.” They said, “When we were there, we could not raise our heads; now he has come here?” They thought he was alive. They told them, “His coffin has come.” Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi went out; Rabbi Ila and Rabbi Chanina did not. (Yuchasin writes: it seems to me that this is Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi—meaning that unqualified Rabbi Chanina is bar Chama, who died before Rav Huna; examine it and you will find this.) Some say Rabbi Ila went out and Rabbi Chanina did not. What is the reason of the one who went out …? What is the reason of the one who did not …? Rav Huna’s skeleton was intact; he did not go out because they had not specified this to him. They said, “Where shall we place him? Let us bring him into Rabbi Chiyya’s cave, for Rav Huna spread Torah”—as we say in the aforementioned chapter Dayyanei Gezerot; Rashi—“and Rabbi Chiyya spread Torah”—as we say in Bava Metzia, “I act so that Torah shall not be forgotten”; see there. “Who will bring him in?”—who will go to bring him for burial beside Rabbi Chiyya? Rav Chaga said, “I shall bring him in, for I had established my learning when I was eighteen years old”—Yuchasin writes that he was eighteen when he learned the entire Talmud from Rav Huna—“I never saw a seminal emission, I served before him”—“I served before Rabbi Chiyya,” Rashi in Ein Yaakov—“and I know his deeds”—Rav Huna’s, Yuchasin. One day his tefillin strap turned over, and he observed forty fasts for it. Rashi explains that the strap’s black side was inward. Rashi in Ein Yaakov says that the letters Shaddai must appear outward in the knot of the head-tefillin strap, but it turned inward toward the head. Yuchasin writes: “He testified concerning Rav Huna that his tefillin strap broke”; Rashi reads “turned over ….” In Adam VeChavah, in the responsa of the Geonim: one whose strap turns over, whether of the head or the arm, must fast because he was negligent; but he is not obliged to fast forty days like Rav Huna, for he did that from great piety. This appears like Rashi’s explanation that it was on Rav Huna’s head. He brought him in. Yehudah lay on his father’s right and Chizkiyahu on his left. Yehudah said to his brother Chizkiyahu, “Arise, for Rav Huna has come.” When he arose, a pillar of fire arose with him. Rav Chaga saw it and was afraid; he, Rav Chaga, set Rav Huna’s coffin upright before the pillar of fire so that it should not harm him. (In Yuchasin, in Rav Sherira Gaon’s epistle: “The reason the exilarch’s house were not punished is that he set Rav Huna’s coffin upright.” It is a scribal error and should read, “The reason Rav Chaga was not punished ….”) Everyone’s eyes can see that this Rav Huna, whom Rabbi Chaga buried in Rabbi Chiyya’s cave, is Rav Huna the Babylonian, whose student Rav Chisda was and to whom Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi deferred. He spread Torah, of whom they said in the Land of Israel, “They have risen from Rav Huna the Babylonian’s academy ….” I was astonished to see in Jerusalem Talmud, Kilayim chapter 9, halakhah 4; Ketubbot, chapter Hanose; Bereshit Rabbah, Noach, chapter 33; and Midrash Kohelet, on “Whatever your hand finds to do,” as follows: Rabbi said, “If Rav Huna the exilarch comes up here, I shall seat him above me.” Once Rabbi Chiyya the Great entered before him and said, “Rav Huna is outside.” Rabbi’s face changed color. He said, “His coffin has come ….” There in the Jerusalem Talmud: “When Rav Huna the exilarch died, they brought him up here. He said, ‘Where shall we put him?’ They said, ‘Let us place him beside Rabbi Chiyya the Great ….’ Who wishes to place him? Rabbi Chanayya said, ‘I shall go in ….’ He found three”—coffins; so in A.A.—“דנין [unresolved], ‘Yehudah my son, behind you’; ‘and no more, Chizkiyah my son ….’ He heard Rabbi Chiyya’s voice saying to his son Yehudah, ‘Make room for Rav Huna’; he sat down ….” It is explicit there that Rabbi Chiyya told Rabbi that Rav Huna the exilarch’s coffin had come. In the aforementioned Midrash Kohelet: Rav Huna the exilarch told us, “When I die, bring me in beside Rabbi Chiyya the Great”; see at length in all the aforementioned places. This is the reverse of the Babylonian Talmud in chapter Megallechin above, where all this happened to Rav Huna the Babylonian. After searching I found that Tosafot, Moed Katan 25, beginning of side a, s.v. “Rabbi Chiyya spread Torah …,” noticed our difficulty. They write: “In the master’s Tosafot the objection is raised that the Jerusalem Talmud implies Rav Huna died before Rabbi Chiyya, for he said to Rabbi Chiyya, ‘His coffin has come’”—it should read, “Rabbi Chiyya said to his teacher, ‘His coffin has come,’” meaning the coffin of Rav Huna the exilarch; newer Talmud editions did not correct it—“while here it implies Rabbi Chiyya died before Rav Huna.” (It is puzzling why they did not notice that the aforementioned Jerusalem Talmud also implies Rabbi Chiyya died before Rav Huna; the Jerusalem Talmud’s words contradict one another on that very page.) “It appears to me that this was another Rav Huna; the one in Rabbi Chiyya’s days is not Rav’s student. However, there is a difficulty: in the Jerusalem Talmud’s account of this incident it says ‘Rav Huna the exilarch.’ According to the Jerusalem Talmud’s account, it would imply that Rabbi Chaga set Rav Huna’s coffin upright so that he would not sit beside the righteous; so too in Rabbenu Chananel’s commentary, ‘Rav Huna the exilarch.’” End of quotation. I saw in Yefeh Mareh, on the aforementioned Kilayim: “It is puzzling: above, Rabbi Chiyya said concerning him, ‘His coffin has come’; thus he died during Rabbi Chiyya’s lifetime. Perhaps there were two earlier Rav Huna exilarchs. From Tosafot in chapter Megallechin it appears that they did not hold there were two exilarchs.” End of quotation. Tosafot’s statement that the Rav Huna in Rabbi Chiyya’s and Rabbi’s days is not Rav’s student is obvious even to a beginner. Rabbi Chiyya said to Rabbi, “Your rival is in Babylonia”—who was that? Rav Huna. Was Rav Huna, Rav’s student, in Rabbi’s time as a rival beside him? See above, Rav Huna the exilarch. For the location of his grave, see Rav Yosef bar Chama.

F) Rav Huna was Rav’s principal student: Shabbat 128a; end of Beitzah, 40a; Bava Kamma 115a; Tosafot, Eruvin 7b; Rashi at the end of chapter Bakhol Mearvin. There, 15, end of side a, Rav said to him, “This scholar resembles one who does not explain the teaching.” In Ketubbot 106, end of side a, he asked Rav, and Rav told him, “He who taught you the Writings did not teach you the Prophets.” In Chullin chapter 7, 95b, he asked Rav, “What if the meat is threaded on a cord?” He answered, “Do not be foolish about meat threaded on a cord.” Pesachim 3b: Rav Huna said in Rabbi’s name; some say, Rav Huna said in Rav’s name. In Shevuot 18a, “Rav Huna said in Rava’s name” should read “in Rav’s name.” According to D.T., “They say in Rav’s house” is Rav Huna, as stated in chapter Parah; in Tosafot, Shabbat 44a, it means “in Rav Huna’s house.” In Sanhedrin chapter 1, 17b, and Tosafot, chapter Keitzad HaRegel, 19a, unqualified “They say in Rav’s house” is in Rav’s name. In Bava Kamma 75a, Rava said to Rav Hamnuna, “You have cut down the elders of Rav’s house”—that is, you defeated the elders of Rav’s house, meaning Rav Huna. Rashi explains otherwise there; see Tosafot. See Yevamot 83b, Rashi and Tosafot, and Bava Batra 153a: it is Rav Huna where it is not proved to be Rav Hamnuna; see his entry and Tosafot. In Zevachim 87a: “They say in Rav’s house: what is Rav Chisda’s reason?” Tosafot writes: although “They say in Rav’s house” is Rav Huna, and Rav Chisda was his student, perhaps Rav Huna too said it and explained its reason; the Talmud fixed it in this wording, “What is Rav Chisda’s reason?” Alternatively, we find Rav Huna accustomed to praising his words, as he said in Gittin, “Chisda is your name and your words are gracious” (see his entry), and in Shabbat, “Why do you not frequent Rav Chisda, whose teachings are sharp?” In Taanit 23b, the pious men of Babylonia are Rav Huna and Rav Chisda. At folio 20b, Rava said to Rafram bar Pappa, “Let the master tell us some of the excellent deeds Rav Huna used to do.” He answered, “I do not remember his youth; I remember his old age. On every cloudy day he would inspect the whole town. He would demolish every weak wall and rebuild it at his own expense if its owner had no means to rebuild. Every Sabbath eve he bought all the remaining vegetables so that they would bring vegetables for the Sabbath meal. When he ate bread he opened the door and said, ‘Whoever needs, let him come and eat’” (see there). From this it appears that he was wealthy and Rav’s blessing was fulfilled. For Megillah 27b says: Rav Huna tied a reed belt around himself and stood before Rav. He asked, “Where is your belt?” He answered, “I had no wine for kiddush and pledged my belt.” He said, “May it be His will that you be covered in silks”—enclosed and covered in robes. When his son Rabbah entered the wedding canopy, Rav Huna, a short man—meaning small of body—went and lay on a bed. His daughters and daughters-in-law came, took off their garments, and threw them over him until he was covered in silks. When Rav heard, he was displeased and said, “Why, when I blessed you, did you not say, ‘The same to the master’?”—you too should be blessed; perhaps it was a favorable hour, and it would have been fulfilled for me too. Tosafot, Bekhorot 44a: “Rav Huna was a short man, as stated in Taanit, chapter of the pious.” End of quotation. This is an error: it is not there, only in the aforementioned Megillah. I do not know whether this is Rav Huna Zuta, for there too his son’s name is Rabbah, or whether the designation distinguishes him from the known Rav Huna. The latter appears so, for Rabbah Zuta was of Nehardea (see his entry); in the Jerusalem Talmud he is called Rav Huna Rabbah. He would light the lamp in honor of the Sabbath: Shabbat 119a. When a case came before him, he assembled ten, so that a splinter of the beam might reach each: Sanhedrin 7b. Shalshelet HaKabbalah, 34b, writes: Rav Huna wrote seventy Torah scrolls, and one was invalid because its width equaled its length. He surely wrote this while dozing and asleep! On the contrary, its principal proper form and fitness is that its length equal its width, as stated in Bava Batra 14a: “The rabbis taught: one does not make a Torah scroll with its length exceeding its circumference or its circumference exceeding its length. Rav Huna wrote seventy Torah scrolls, and it came out right for him only once. Rav Acha bar Yaakov wrote one, and it came out right. The rabbis set their eyes upon him, and he died.” End of quotation. In Berakhot chapter 1, 5b, Rav Huna had four hundred jars of wine that soured. Rav Yehudah, brother of Rav Salla the Pious, and the rabbis entered before him. They said, “Let the master examine his deeds.” He answered, “Am I suspect in your eyes?” They said, “Is the Holy One, blessed be He, suspect of executing judgment without justice …?” They said that the master did not give vine branches to his sharecropper. He replied, “But he steals them all from me.” They said, “Steal after a thief, and taste the taste!” He undertook to give them to him, and it became wine again. Some say the vinegar rose in price and was sold for the price of wine. It seems to me that he had so much wine because he was careful about sanctifying the day, as above, just as Rabbi Zakkai’s mother and Rabbi Zakkai merited leaving much wine because he was careful about sanctifying the day, as stated in chapter Benei Hair. In Berakhot 42a, Rav Huna ate thirteen loaves, of a size of three to a kav, and did not bless. Rav Nachman said to him, “These were eaten out of hunger!” See Rashi there. In Chullin 112a: he was delicate. After Rav Huna’s death his wife had a case before Rav Nachman (see his entry).

G) Between Rav Huna and Rav, the law follows Rav (see his entry). Between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda, the law follows Rav Huna, who was his teacher: Tosafot, Berakhot 24b; Bava Metzia 7 and 33a; Kiddushin 50a; Menachot 42a. See Eruvin 62b; Berakhot 34a. Asheri, chapter Mefannin: the law follows Rav Huna, for Rav Chisda was a student before him. The law follows Rav Assi against Rav Huna (see his entry). Between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman, we hold like Rav Huna in prohibitory matters and Rav Nachman in civil matters; see Ketubbot, beginning of folio 13, 51a, 68b. Responsa Chavvot Yair, section 94, requires examination. Between Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah, Rosh, chapter Hagozel Etzim, writes that the law follows Rav Huna, because he was Rav Yehudah’s teacher; see there, section 10. Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam, gate 3, section 20, says he was his colleague. Rashi likewise writes at the end of chapter Bakhol Mearvin that Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah were Rav’s students; thus he was his colleague. The law follows Rav Huna against Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav (see above).

H) Rabbi Abba was his student (see his entry). In Gittin 46, end of side b, he said to Rav Huna, “You taught us, our master.” In Chullin 9a he asked Rav Huna; in Bava Kamma 102a he sat before Rav Huna. In Sukkah 13b; Shabbat 5a, 98a; and Bekhorot 38b, he reported Rav Huna. We find in Zevachim 36b that Rav Huna raised an objection to Rabbi Abba. Abba bar Avimi was in his time. Rabbi Abba bar Zavda was his student. Abba, Shmuel’s father, raised an objection; this requires examination there. Abba bar Huna (see his entry). In Rabbi Abbahu’s name: Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot chapter 8. Avimi of Hagronya in his name. He passed Rabbi Avin the carpenter’s doorway. Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Huna sat before Rabbi Yirmeyah. Rabbi Avina was his student. Rav Avya the Elder asked him. Rabbi Oshaya: see Hoshaya shortly below. And Rabbi Acha. Rav Acha bar Yaakov was his student. Rav Acha bar Huna. Rav Acha bar Pappa before him. Rav Acha bar Yosef was his student. Rabbi Acha bar Chanina was his student. Rabbi Acha bar Azza before him. Achi the irrigator brought out for him [אפיק ליה; object unspecified]. Rabbi Ila did not go out to meet his coffin (see above). Rabbi Elazar asked him (I did not find it). In Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Yose HaGelili’s name. Rabbi Ammi went out to meet his coffin. Rabbi Ammi bar Abba in his name. He reported Rav Assi. Rabbi Assi went out to meet his coffin. He asked Rav Ashi. “We were in Rav Huna’s house”; he raised an objection to Rav Ashi; Rav Ashi said, “When I stood before Rav Huna ….” This is the earlier Rav Ashi: Rav Huna died before Rav Yehudah; Rava was born when Rav Yehudah died, and the later Rav Ashi was born when Rava died. Rabbi Benaya in his name. In Rabbi Binyamin bar Levi’s name. Rav Giddel was his student. Rav Giddel bar Minyomi before him. In Rabbi Giddel of Naresh’s name. Geniva in his time. Rabbi Daniel bar Katina in his name. Rabbi Huna bar Katina in his time; and Rav Huna bar Chiyya (see his entry). Rav Hoshaya asked Rav Huna Rabbah: Bekhorot 37, end of side b. Rav Hamnuna (see his entry); it appears that one was his teacher and one his student. Rav Zavda, father of his student Rabbi Abba. Rav Zavdi in his name. The pair from Adiabene were present at his death (see their entry). Mar Zutra in his name. Rabbi Zeira was his student. Rabbi Zeira [זעירא] in his name, and Rav Huna in his name (requires examination). Zeiri (see his entry). Rabbi Zerika in his name. In Rabbi Huna’s name. Rav Huna, Rabbi Chizkiyah, and Rabbi Pinchas went to visit Rabbi Yose: Jerusalem Talmud, Gittin chapter 6, halakhah 7. Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin was his student. He reported Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba. Chiyya bar Rav (see above). Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi (see his entry). In Chilfai’s name. Rabbi Chelbo was his student. And Rabbi Chilkiyah bar Tuvyah. He reported Rabbi Chama bar Gurya. Rabbi Chana bar Katina was his student (I did not find it). Rabbi Chana bar Chanilai. Rabbi Chana bar Chinena asked him. Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi did not go out to meet his coffin (see above). In Rabbi Chanina bar Yitzchak’s name. He reported Rabbi Chanina: Shabbat 122a; Eruvin 79a. He said to Rav Chanan bar Rava. Rav Chanan bar Molada in his name. Chak Bisha stole a cloak and sold it; he came to Rav Huna: Bava Kamma 115a. Rav Chananel (see his entry). Rav Chisda: whether he was his student (see his entry). Rav Yehudah was his student or colleague (see above, the ruling of law). Rabbi Yehudah, brother of Rav Salla the Pious (see above). He ruled for Rabbi Yehudah bar Zavdi’s brother (see his entry). He reported Rabbi Yochanan: Berakhot 24b; Rabbi Yochanan said to him: Moed Katan 20a. Rabbi Yochanan ben Molada said in Rav Huna’s name. Rabbi Yonah Botzra’ah asked him. In Rabbi Yusta bar Shunem’s name. In Rabbi Yose’s name: Eikhah Rabbah, on “Great among the nations”; Kohelet, on “What has been already is”; that matter in Vayikra Rabbah chapter 27. Also Bereshit Rabbah chapter 9, “ס״ה,” chapter 5 [compressed locators as printed]. Shemot Rabbah chapter 52; Vayikra Rabbah chapter 23, in Rabbi Yosef’s name. Rabbi Yosef before him and in his name: Bereshit Rabbah chapter 12. Maimonides writes: Rav Yosef received from Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah. He reported Rabbi Yannai. Rabbi Yannai of Cappadocia before him. In Yaavetz’s name. And Rabbi Yitzchak, son of Rav Yehudah. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chanina in his name. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in his name, and he asked him. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ashyan said in Rav Huna’s name. Yirmeyah bar Abba (see his entry). In Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yose’s name. In Rabbi Kahana bar Malkhya’s name: Bereshit Rabbah, Noach, chapter 31. The first Rav Kahana was his colleague—so writes Yuchasin; requires examination. Rabbi Kahana, Rabbi Yehudah’s brother, before him. Levi bar Shmuel in his time. Levi bar Buta before Rav Huna. In Rabbi Meir’s name: Bereshit Rabbah chapter 45. Rabbi Menashe bar Zevid before him. Rabbi Menashya bar Gada said in Rav Huna’s name. Merimar was his student. Rav Nachman bar Yaakov was his colleague (see his entry). In Bava Kamma 9a, Rav Nachman raised an objection to Rav Huna. In Eruvin 77a, Rav Huna said in Rav Nachman’s name. Niyuli in his name. Rav Sechora said in Rav Huna’s name. In Mar Ukvan’s name. Rav Anan sent to Rav Huna, “Our colleague,” and Rav Huna was angry with him. In Rav Pedayah’s name. And Rabbi Pinchas (see above, Chizkiyah). In bar Kappara’s name. Rav was his teacher (see above). In Rava’s name—requires examination; see his entry. Rava bar Natan said to him. Rabbah bar Nachmani received from him and was his student, as is proved at the end of Bava Batra and in chapter Kol HaGet. At the end of chapter Bakhol Mearvin, 40b, he said: “When I was in Rav Huna’s house, we asked a question and he did not have it; when I came to Rav Yehudah’s house ….” Raavad likewise writes in his objections—so Yuchasin writes under Rabbah. Rabbah said: Rav Huna said in Rav Nachman’s name, Eruvin 77a. He asked Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah: Eruvin 17a. Concerning Rabbah, son of Rav Huna, Raavad writes that he received from Rav Huna. Rabbah bar Abbahu. Rabbah bar Chakola. Rav Huna said in Rabbi’s name: Beitzah 16b; Pesachim 3b; Kiddushin 60b; Ketubbot 68b. It is difficult to emend it to “said in Rav’s name.” Rami bar Abba said in Rav Huna’s name. Rami bar Yechezkel sent to him. Rami bar Chama in his name, and Rav Huna in his name. And Rami bar Shmuel. Rafram bar Pappa told Rava of his deeds (see above). And Rabbi Shabbetai, in Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah’s name. Shmuel asked him (see above). Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak asked him and reported in his name. Rav Huna said in his name—requires examination. Rav Shmuel bar Sheva said in Rav Huna’s name. In Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yose’s name. Rav Sheshet was his student. “Rav Huna said in Rav Sheshet’s name”: see his entry; a scribal error. Rabbi Tanchuma in his name.
